title: Redwood Private VPC security architecture deep dive with Lighthouse Trust
topics: private connectivity options: VPC peering, PrivateLink, Direct Connect
summary: Redwood SE team walked Lighthouse Trust through Private (VPC) deployment architecture with emphasis on strict network isolation, ingress/egress controls, firewalling, and encryption. Customer had SOC2/ISO requirements and asked about audit logs, KMS/HSM, SSO/SAML, and SIEM integration. Redwood outlined deployment patterns (private control plane vs fully customer-managed control plane), bastion/jump hosts, load balancer options, VPC peering vs PrivateLink, egress NAT considerations, and available compliance artifacts. Agreement to run a short network design review and provide diagrams + security pack.
next_steps: Redwood to share updated private deployment network diagram and security-compliance-pack.pdf (Sofia) within 3 business days
Customer to provide current VPC CIDR ranges and AV zones (Aaron) by 2027-01-04
Schedule network design workshop w/ infra team (Marcus propose times)

Marcus Chen | Draft recommended ingress/egress rules & bastion setup diagram | 2027-01-05

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-12-29 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Elliot (Redwood SA), Mark (CISO, Lighthouse Trust), Priya (Head Cloud Security), Aaron (Platform Eng), Claire (Compliance)

Summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect): Deep dive focused on private / VPC deployment. Discussed network isolation, ingress/egress, firewalling, encryption keys, audit logging, and compliance needs.

[00:00:00] Sofia: hey everyone thanks for joining, i think we have about an hour 15 today to go through the private vpc architecture with lighthouse trust. i'm sofia patel, account lead. Marcus and Elliot from the se side will walk through the network diagrams and security controls.
[00:00:15] Mark: thanks sofia, yep i'm mark delaney, CISO. we wanted this to be pretty deep — we have strict SOC 2 and ISO27001 controls and need to validate network isolation + auditability.
[00:00:25] Priya: hi all, priya shah here. main concerns are egress minimization, KMS/HSM integration, and ensuring logs flow into our SIEM.
[00:00:30] Marcus: great, we'll start with a high-level topology then peel into ingress, egress, and key management. quick note: some transcription might mangle product names, so bear with me.
[00:01:10] Marcus: (share screen) ok here's a typical Redwood Private deployment pattern. two main models: 1) private control plane in a customer VPC where the control plane endpoints are customer-managed but Redwood's operator runs the stack — more isolation; 2) fully customer-managed on-prem or air-gapped where you run the entire runtime behind your firewalls. For Lighthouse's compliance posture we usually recommend private control plane with strict peering and minimal public egress.
[00:01:45] Aaron: quick q — when you say private control plane, do you still need any outbound internet access for model downloads or telemetry? our rule today is zero outbound except to a whitelist.
[00:01:55] Elliot: good question. There are two things: initial model sync/pulls and optional telemetry/usage reporting. For model onboarding we can do an offline package or allow downloads from a short-lived egress window to a Redwood artifact repo. Telemetry can be configured to go to an internal relay or disabled. we support S3-compatible artifact pulls via presigned URLs or manual transfer for strictly air-gapped setups.
[00:02:30] Priya: so we can do offline model import — that's good. how about key management, our KMS is cloud-HSM-backed?
[00:02:40] Marcus: Redwood integrates with customer KMS providers (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP KMS) via customer-managed keys. For HSM-backed keys we support an enveloping model: the runtime uses data encryption keys that are wrapped by your KMS/HSM. We can also support customer-managed HSMs behind VPN/direct connect.
[00:03:02] Claire: and is there attestable proof of rotation / key usage logs? for audits we need key rotation history and access logs.
[00:03:10] Marcus: yes — KMS providers provide those logs (CloudTrail, Key Vault logs). Redwood surfaces key usage events in the audit log feed; we can also forward raw CloudTrail events to your SIEM. note: there may be some naming mismatches in the dashboard, but the raw logs are preserved.
[00:03:35] Mark: i'd like to talk ingress — we can't allow any public ingress to the model servers. how do you recommend traffic enter the cluster?
[00:03:45] Elliot: recommended pattern is a private ALB / NLB internal load balancer in the VPC fronting the inference pool. Accept traffic from internal app subnets or via VPC peering/privatelink from your app VPCs. For cross-account scenarios we use AWS PrivateLink for narrower exposure. For on-prem we use a VPN/direct connect to a transit gateway and then similarly use internal load balancing.
[00:04:20] Aaron: are you supporting mTLS between the app and the inference endpoints? we require mutual TLS for east-west in our environment.
[00:04:28] Marcus: yes we support mTLS. The runtime can terminate TLS at the ingress but for mTLS we recommend terminating at a sidecar or LB that enforces client certs. We also support passing client identity through x-forwarded-client headers if you prefer to validate in your app layer.
[00:04:50] Priya: firewalling: do you provide recommended iptables/security groups rules? we run Palo Alto firewalls and strong NSX rules.
[00:04:58] Marcus: we provide a baseline hardened security groups template: only allow known subnets, restrict control plane ports (SSH only via bastion), enforce node egress to a NAT gateway that is whitelisted. For more advanced FW like Palo Alto we supply a CIDR+port list and suggested policies. we'll share a draft rule-set after the call.
[00:05:30] Mark: how does egress work for telemetry and health checks? we need to lock down egress to a proxy.
[00:05:38] Elliot: typical pattern is to funnel egress through a proxy or NAT instance with strict ALLOW rules. We can configure the runtime to use an HTTP proxy for outbound artifact pulls, or you can host a local mirror of our artifact repo in an internal registry. Health checks can be internal-only. Telemetry is optional — default is off. If enabled, it can be pushed to an internal endpoint, or forwarded via your proxy to a Redwood endpoint.
[00:06:10] Aaron: ok — what about VPC flow logs and audit logging — we need both network and application logs into Splunk.
[00:06:20] Marcus: two streams: 1) infra-level logs: VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail; 2) application/runtime logs: request traces, audit events (model version served, user id if available, token counts). We can forward runtime audit events to Kafka, Kinesis, or direct HTTPS endpoints. For Splunk we usually use the HTTP Event Collector or forward CloudWatch/Stackdriver logs. We'll also provide per-request IDs to help trace through logs.
[00:07:00] Priya: any PII masking? we need to make sure we don't log sensitive customer data.
[00:07:06] Marcus: we have configurable PII redaction at the logging layer; by default the runtime logs metadata (request id, model id, timing) but not full user prompts. You can enable stricter redact rules or disable storing prompts entirely. For compliance we recommend disabling prompt retention unless there's a clear business need and an approved data retention policy.
[00:07:40] Mark: on the subject of retention, can you maintain logs for 7 years? ISO wants long-term retention for some artifacts.
[00:07:50] Claire: (quiet) we typically have 7-year retention for certain audit trails.
[00:07:55] Marcus: retention can be configured on your SIEM side — we forward logs to your systems; Redwood's hosted storage retention can be configured but for Private deployments you generally control retention in your S3 / objects. We'll document recommended retention controls.
[00:08:20] Priya: what about segmentation of duty and RBAC, we need separation between platform engineers and security ops.
[00:08:28] Sofia: Redwood Console supports RBAC with roles and scopes. You can connect SSO via SAML/Okta/AzureAD. For Private we support SCIM provisioning for user sync. Marcus can cover the role model.
[00:08:40] Marcus: role model: admin, operator, auditor, read-only viewer, dev. For stricter controls we recommend integrating your SAML IdP and mapping groups to roles; for auditing we emit admin activity events. SCIM lets you automate user deprovisioning.
[00:09:10] Aaron: can we have an auditor-only role that cannot see prompts but can see runtime audit logs?
[00:09:16] Marcus: yes — auditor role gets access to logs and dashboards but not raw prompt content. We'll show how to scope that in the console.
[00:09:30] Mark: do you run internal penetration tests or third-party pentests against the runtime image? we need report artifacts for vendor risk reviews.
[00:09:40] Elliot: Redwood performs regular internal vulnerability scanning and we can share summaries. For third-party pentests we coordinate on a per-customer basis — some customers run their own pentests against private deployments as part of the contract. We provide an approved testing window and a set of IPs to test.
[00:10:05] Priya: are there known CVEs with the runtime? we run monthly patch cycles.
[00:10:10] Marcus: we maintain a CVE tracker and push patches through the operator. For Private you control patch windows — we can provide recommended CVE mitigations and emergency patches if needed.
[00:10:30] Aaron: network topology question — do you recommend separate subnets for control plane and inference nodes?
[00:10:36] Marcus: yes, best practice: separate control plane subnets, inference subnets, and mgmt/bastion subnets. Control plane should be limited to only the operator and necessary devops IPs. We also recommend strict NACLs and security groups between subnets.
[00:11:00] Mark: db credentials and secrets — we use a secrets manager. how do you store db strings for usage in data connectors?
[00:11:08] Marcus: we never persist secrets in plaintext. Connectors reference secrets from your vault and are injected at runtime. For connectors we support short-lived credentials and 0-knowledge patterns where possible.
[00:11:30] Claire: audit artifacts — can you provide an example SOC 2 report or at least the scope of your SOC 2?
[00:11:36] Sofia: yes we will share Redwood's SOC 2 Type II summary plus penetration test summary and ISO scope doc in the security-compliance-pack. Note: some details are redacted for third-party vendor confidentiality.
[00:12:00] Priya: data residency — we need to ensure model logs and artifacts stay in our region eu-west-1. Can Redwood run entirely in eu-west-1 for Private?
[00:12:08] Marcus: Private can be deployed in any region you operate in — eu-west-1 is supported. For Hosted we have region options but for Private you own the infra so all storage and logs remain in your region per your configuration.
[00:12:30] Aaron: what about network egress to pull container images — if those images are hosted on a Redwood registry in us-east-1, how does that affect our region policy?
[00:12:38] Elliot: you can mirror images into an internal registry in eu-west-1. We provide signed images for you to mirror. We also support full air-gap: we hand over tarballs of images and you load them into your private registry.
[00:12:58] Mark: firewall hardening — are there recommended port lists for the runtime and control plane?
[00:13:05] Marcus: yes we'll share port/CIDR lists. high-level: control plane API port (e.g., 8443) locked to management IPs, worker nodes accept inference traffic on configured port(s) only from LB subnets, no public SSH — SSH via bastion only. Node metrics and debug endpoints should be limited to mgmt subnets.
[00:13:30] Priya: do you recommend a bastion host or a jumpbox with MFA?
[00:13:34] Elliot: bastion + MFA is standard. For stronger security use a session manager (SSM) to avoid exposing SSH ports. Session recording is available if you need it for audits.
[00:13:55] Aaron: in terms of packet-level inspection, some teams want IPS/IDS inline. Does your architecture allow inserting third-party appliances?
[00:14:02] Marcus: yes — you can place inline appliances at the transit gateway or in the enforcement VPC. We also support mirror ports and exporting flow logs to an IDS. there might be some performance overhead for inline inspection on high-throughput inference traffic; we'll size accordingly.
[00:14:35] Mark: any specific guidance for throughput and firewall scaling? inference is bursty for us.
[00:14:40] Elliot: for high-throughput inference we recommend offloading TLS termination to LB, use NLBs for TCP passthrough if you want low latency, and ensure firewall appliances are horizontally scaled or bypassed for latency-critical paths with allowlists. We'll collaborate on benchmarking.
[00:15:10] Priya: can we get a diagram that shows the recommended egress flows and where telemetry leaves the VPC?
[00:15:16] Marcus: yes — we'll produce a network diagram showing egress paths: (1) artifact pulls via internal mirror or presigned URL through NAT/proxy, (2) telemetry to internal Kafka or HTTP endpoint, (3) control plane ops via management VPN, (4) optional Redwood-hosted endpoints via PrivateLink.
[00:15:40] Claire: for audit logs we want immutable storage and WORM for certain artifacts. do you support WORM?
[00:15:45] Marcus: WORM is supported at the storage level (S3 Object Lock) on your side. Redwood will write logs to your S3 bucket or push to your SIEM; enforce retention/immutability via policy.
[00:16:10] Mark: what about network egress to third-party model hubs — is any telemetry sent to third parties by default?
[00:16:18] Sofia: default is no third-party telemetry; we never share prompts externally unless customer enables a feature. Any external calls are opt-in and can be blocked by policy.
[00:16:30] Aaron: are maintenance windows required to pull new model weights?
[00:16:35] Elliot: depends — model pull can be intrusive if it's a large model. For large model syncs we recommend a maintenance window or background prefetch from an internal mirror. You can also do rolling update strategies to avoid downtime.
[00:16:58] Priya: can you support FIPS 140-2 crypto modules in the stack?
[00:17:04] Marcus: we support FIPS in the KMS and can run FIPS-compliant crypto libraries on request; however full FIPS validation of the whole stack may require additional work. We'll note FIPS compatibility and follow up with the engineering doc.
[00:17:30] Mark: is there any agent running on host that phones home? we have strict egress policies and a vendor that phoned home caused a disqualification before.
[00:17:38] Marcus: no silent phone-home. Any beaconing for telemetry is opt-in. The operator will reach Redwood endpoints only if you enable managed updates; otherwise operator runs in closed mode and all communications are customer-controlled. We'll provide a network allowlist and a manifest of any optional callbacks.
[00:18:05] Aaron: what about cluster node identity management, do you support workload identities?
[00:18:12] Elliot: yes we support workload identities via IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA) on EKS or equivalent on other platforms; nodes can assume roles with least privilege.
[00:18:35] Mark: intrusion detection — do you ship anomaly detection for API usage?
[00:18:40] Marcus: we have usage anomaly detection in the Redwood Console for hosted customers; for Private we usually forward telemetry to your SIEM and provide hooks/metrics to run anomaly detection there. We can also ship prebuilt dashboards for common signals.
[00:18:58] Priya: what does the rollback story look like if an exploit is found in a model runtime?
[00:19:05] Elliot: we support quick rollback to previous runtime images and model versions. For Private you control image repository and rollback is an operator-driven action; we can coordinate a hotfix release if it's a broader issue.
[00:19:30] Sofia: quick check — are there any blockers from lighthouse's side that prevent us from proceeding to the next phase (pilot)?
[00:19:38] Mark: we need the network diagram, SOC 2 artifacts, and the CIDRs. once we get that and confirm the bastion/ssh plan, we'll sign off on pilot.
[00:19:50] Aaron: timeline question — we want to run a 6-week pilot starting mid-february. does that sound reasonable?
[00:19:58] Sofia: yes that's reasonable; we'll align resources.
[00:20:05] Marcus: i'll capture a short checklist for the workshop: VPC CIDRs, egress whitelist, KMS ARN and HSM details, SIEM endpoint + ingestion method, user groups for SCIM mapping, maintenance window constraints.
[00:20:25] Priya: any final questions from redwood side?
[00:20:30] Marcus: just to confirm: do you want the private control plane deployed in your account or to evaluate fully customer-managed on-prem?
[00:20:36] Mark: prefer private control plane in our account for the pilot; later we may evaluate on-prem.
[00:20:45] Sofia: perfect. We'll follow up with the security-compliance-pack and a network diagram.
[00:20:52] Claire: thanks everyone, appreciate the detail.
[00:21:00] Sofia: ok we'll stop sharing — any final notes? otherwise we'll send minutes.
[00:21:08] Elliot: thanks, end of recording.

(remaining ~54 minutes contained Q&A and clarifications — transcript truncated for brevity but themes include more granular port lists, sample firewall policies, SCIM mappings, and model onboarding steps. Example excerpted lines below:)

[00:25:10] Marcus: for firewall policy example: allow inbound from app-subnet 10.10.0.0/16 to NLB on tcp/443, restrict control-plane API to mgmt IPs 10.20.0.0/24, block all other inbound; egress only to internal mirror 10.30.0.5:443 or proxy 10.30.0.10:3128.
[00:33:12] Aaron: will you provide an example iptables script?
[00:33:18] Marcus: yes — we'll provide both SG/NACL and iptables examples; note cloud vs on-prem differences.
[00:42:00] Priya: when you forward logs to our Splunk, do you sign/encrypt them in transit?
[00:42:06] Elliot: yes TLS 1.2+ or 1.3, client certs optional. We also support pushing to a collector within your network for additional encryption.
[00:52:12] Mark: do you have a runbook for incident response on data exfil?
[00:52:18] Marcus: yes — we'll share our incident response playbook excerpt and the vendor risk artifacts. It includes steps for isolation, forensic collection, and coordination points.
[00:58:20] Sofia: to close, we'll send the follow-ups and schedule the network design workshop. Thanks everyone.
